title: Contains Duplicate II
directAnswer: Return true if there exist two equal values within index distance k — i.e. nums[i] == nums[j] and |i − j| ≤ k. The clean answer is a hash map of value → most-recent index: when you re-see a value, check if the gap to its last index is ≤ k. Equivalently, slide a window of size k holding a set of the last k values. Both are O(n) time; the window is O(min(n, k)) space.

remember.pattern: Hash map of last index, OR sliding-window set of size k
rules: Always **overwrite** `last[x] = i` even on a non-match — the nearest previous index gives the smallest gap, the best chance of `≤ k`.
Compare `i - last[x] <= k`, not `< k` — distance exactly `k` is allowed.
Edge case `k == 0`: no two distinct indices can be within distance 0, so the answer is always `false` (handle naturally, the gap is ≥ 1).
**Duplicate value alone is not enough** — the indices must be close. This is Contains Duplicate plus a distance constraint.
The sliding-window variant keeps a set of the **last k** elements; remove `nums[i-k]` as the window slides to cap space at `O(k)`.
whenToUse: Find a repeated element within a bounded index/time window
'Have I seen this recently?' rather than 'ever?'
Stream/array problems with a 'within the last k' locality constraint
antiSignals: Any duplicate anywhere counts → plain Contains Duplicate (a set, no distance)
Values must be close in VALUE too (|nums[i]-nums[j]| ≤ t) → Contains Duplicate III, needs buckets/TreeSet
Need the actual pair, not a boolean → store indices and return them
Window over a sum/length, not equality → different sliding-window template
remember.takeaway: Contains Duplicate II = Contains Duplicate + a distance constraint. Keep the most recent index of each value (overwrite always) and check the gap, or maintain a set of the last k values. The 'most recent index' insight — that overwriting beats keeping the first index — is the interview discriminator.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you fold the index-distance constraint into a hash map cleanly — specifically whether you realize you should keep the MOST RECENT index of each value, not the first.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Storing the first occurrence index and never updating it, which can report a gap larger than k even when a closer pair exists; or using strict < k instead of <= k.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Offer both the value→last-index map and the fixed-size sliding-window set, explain the space trade-off, and connect it forward to Contains Duplicate III's value-window generalization.

problemStatement: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return `true` if there are two ***distinct indices*** `i` and `j` in the array such that `nums[i] == nums[j]` and `abs(i - j) <= k`.
understanding: We need two equal values whose positions are at most k apart. It is not enough for a value to repeat — the repetition must happen within a sliding index window of width k. With k ≥ array length this degenerates to plain 'are there any duplicates'; with k = 0 it is always false.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the distance condition |i - j| <= k inclusive of k?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, ≤ k. A gap of exactly k counts as a match. I'll use <= rather than <.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What happens when k is 0?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Two distinct indices have a gap of at least 1, which can never be ≤ 0, so the answer is always false. The code handles it naturally without a special case.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can values be negative or very large?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, up to ±10⁹, so I'll key the hash map by the integer value directly — no array-indexing tricks that assume a small non-negative range.

clarifyingQuestions.question: If k exceeds the array length, does it just become Contains Duplicate?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Effectively yes — every pair is within distance k, so any duplicate at all returns true. Both my solutions handle that without a branch.

Every repeated value is exactly distance 3 apart, which exceeds k = 2.
Distinct indices 0 and 1 have gap 1 > 0. k = 0 can never match.

approaches.name: Hash Map of Last Index (Optimal, simplest)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this — it's the cleanest. Stress 'I keep the MOST RECENT index of each value'.
hints: Plain Contains Duplicate uses a set: 'have I seen x before?'. Here you also need to know HOW LONG ago. What should the map's value be so you can answer that?
Map value → the last index where it appeared. When you re-see x, the gap is i − last[x]; if that's ≤ k you're done.
Crucially, always overwrite last[x] = i, even when the gap was too big — the nearest previous occurrence gives the smallest possible future gap.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Single pass, O(1) average map operations per element → O(n) time. The map can hold up to n distinct values → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Walk the array once, maintaining a hash map from each value to **the most recent index** at which it occurred. At position `i` with value `x`, if `x` is already in the map and `i − last[x] ≤ k`, we've found a qualifying pair and return true. Otherwise we update `last[x] = i` and continue.

**Why 'most recent index' and not 'first index'.** This is the subtle heart of the problem. Suppose `x` appears at indices 0, 4, and 5 with `k = 1`. If we stored only the *first* index 0 and never updated it, then at index 4 we'd compute gap `4 > 1` (no match) and at index 5 gap `5 > 1` (no match) — and wrongly conclude false, even though indices 4 and 5 are distance 1 apart. By **always overwriting** `last[x]` with the current index, the comparison at index 5 uses `last[x] = 4`, giving gap `1 ≤ 1` → true. The nearest previous occurrence is always the one most likely to satisfy the distance bound, so keeping it is both correct and optimal.

**Why this reduces to Contains Duplicate when k is large.** If `k ≥ n − 1`, then *any* repeat has a gap ≤ k, so the first time we ever re-see a value we return true — exactly plain Contains Duplicate. The distance check simply never rejects. This is a good sanity check to mention: Contains Duplicate II strictly generalizes Contains Duplicate, with `k = ∞` recovering the original.

**Why `≤ k` and why k = 0 is automatically false.** Two *distinct* indices differ by at least 1. So when `k = 0` the test `i − last[x] ≤ 0` can never hold (the gap is always ≥ 1), and we correctly return false with no special-casing. Using `≤` rather than `<` matters: a gap of exactly `k` is a valid match per the spec, and `<` would miss the boundary case like `[1,2,3,1], k = 3`.

**Why we don't need the value's full history.** We never care about *all* the places `x` appeared — only the closest one behind us. That's why a single integer per value suffices and the map stays a flat value→index table rather than value→list-of-indices.
approaches.insight: The leap from Contains Duplicate is replacing the set ('seen ever?') with a map to the *last position* ('seen how recently?'). Recency, not mere existence, is the quantity the distance constraint demands — and the smallest gap always comes from the nearest prior occurrence, which is exactly why we overwrite.

approaches.name: Sliding Window — Set of the Last k Values
approaches.whenToMention: Bring up when the interviewer asks to bound memory: this caps space at O(min(n, k)) instead of O(n).
hints: Instead of remembering every value ever seen, only remember the values in the current window of the last k indices. If the incoming value is already in that window, it's a duplicate within distance k.
Maintain a set of the values at indices [i-k, i-1]. Before adding nums[i], check membership; after, evict nums[i-k] so the window never exceeds size k.
The set's size is bounded by k, so this trades the O(n) map for O(k) memory.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each element is added and removed from the set at most once → O(n) total set operations, each O(1) average. The set holds at most k elements → O(min(n, k)) space.
approaches.explanation:
This variant reframes the problem as a literal **sliding window of width k over indices**. We keep a hash set containing exactly the values currently inside the window `[i − k, i − 1]`. When we arrive at index `i`, the question 'is there an equal value within distance k behind me?' becomes simply 'is `nums[i]` already in the set?'.

**Why the window size is exactly k.** A pair `(i, j)` qualifies when `|i − j| ≤ k`. Looking backward from `i`, the eligible partners are at indices `i − 1, i − 2, …, i − k` — that's `k` positions. So the set must hold precisely those `k` values. Before processing `i`, if `i > k` we evict the value that has just fallen out of the window, `nums[i − k]`, keeping the set size capped at `k`. This eviction is what bounds memory at `O(k)` rather than `O(n)`.

**Why a set, not a map.** Within the window we don't need indices at all — membership is sufficient, because everything in the set is by construction within distance k. The window structure encodes the distance constraint *positionally*, so the value alone answers the question. That's the conceptual difference from approach 1: approach 1 stores positions and computes gaps; this one bakes the gap into which elements are present.

**Why this matters when k is small relative to n.** If `n = 10⁵` but `k = 10`, the map approach still allocates up to `10⁵` entries, while the window holds at most `10`. For memory-constrained or streaming scenarios — where you can only retain a recent buffer — the sliding window is the right tool. The trade-off is a touch more bookkeeping (the eviction step) and slightly worse constant factors from the extra remove operations.

**Why eviction uses `nums[i − k]` and the guard `i ≥ k`.** When `i` reaches `k`, index `i − k = 0` is the one leaving the window of the next step, so we remove its value first. For `i < k` the window hasn't filled yet and there's nothing to evict — hence the guard. Getting this index off by one (`i − k` vs `i − k − 1`) is the classic bug; anchoring on 'the window covers the last k indices' keeps it straight.
approaches.insight: When a constraint is 'within the last k', a fixed-width sliding window literally is the constraint — membership in the window answers the question with no arithmetic. Choose this over the global map whenever memory must stay proportional to the window, not the whole stream.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Keeping the first index instead of the most recent
commonMistakesDetailed.why: On nums=[1,2,1,1], k=1 storing only the first index of 1 (=0) makes every later 1 compute a gap from 0, missing the adjacent 1's at indices 2 and 3. Always overwrite.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Strict less-than on the distance
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The spec allows |i-j| == k. Using < k fails nums=[1,2,3,1], k=3 where the matching pair is exactly distance 3 apart.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: if (prev != null && i - prev < k) return true;
commonMistakesDetailed.good: if (prev != null && i - prev <= k) return true;

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sliding-window eviction off-by-one
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The element that leaves a width-k window at step i is at index i-k-1 (since the window covers i-1 down to i-k). Removing nums[i-k] evicts a still-valid partner one step early.

patternNote: Hash map of last index (recency), or a fixed-width sliding-window set. Recognise it whenever 'duplicate' is qualified by 'within the last k' — proximity, not mere existence. The recency-overwrite insight and the window-eviction index are the two implementation discriminators.
